page7_img_2.png.title: Branch activity vs. post-release defects (Windows Vista)
page7_img_2.png.description: Line plot (Figure 2) shows the modeled relationship between branch activity (x-axis: min → median → max) and change in post-release defects (y-axis, normalized so 100% = median). The solid black line is the fitted prediction and the green dashed and red dotted lines are the 95% confidence bounds, all rising roughly linearly: at the minimum branch activity the model predicts about 85% (±2.9%) of median defects, while at the maximum it predicts about 159% (±11%) of median defects. In other words, increasing branch activity is associated with substantially more post-release failures (up to ≈59% higher at the observed maximum), with uncertainty shown by the plotted confidence intervals.

page8_img_1.png.title: R² model fit for architectural vs. organizational mismatch (Vista vs Windows 7)
page8_img_1.png.description: Table of model-fit (R²) values showing how much variance in branch quality (post-release failures) is explained by architectural mismatch, organizational mismatch, and both combined for Windows Vista and Windows 7. For Vista the values are: Arch mismatch = 0.426**, Org mismatch = 0.543**, Org+Arch = 0.594**; for Windows 7: Arch = 0.308**, Org = 0.321**, Org+Arch = 0.385**. Double asterisks denote statistical significance (p < 0.01); the numbers indicate organizational mismatch explains more variance than architectural mismatch in both releases, and the combined model provides the highest R² in each case.

page9_img_1.png.title: Effect of organizational and architectural mismatch on branch failures (Vista vs Windows 7)
page9_img_1.png.description: Table summarizing the modeled effect of organizational (Managers, Leads, Engineers) and architectural (Components, Subcomponents) mismatch on branch post-release failures for Windows Vista and Windows 7. For each metric the table reports the projected percent of failures at the metric's minimum and maximum (normalized to 100% at the median) with ± uncertainty (e.g., Managers in Vista: 100±5% at min, 135±24% at max; Engineers in Vista: 65±8% at min, 217±24% at max). Architectural metrics show smaller maximum effects (Components: Vista 120±8%, Subcomponents: Vista 130±9%) than organizational metrics, indicating that increases in organizational mismatch are associated with larger increases in predicted post-release failures than equivalent increases in architectural mismatch.

page2_img_1.png.title: Example branch tree showing families, depths, and changes for foo.dll and bar.dll
page2_img_1.png.description: A schematic branch‑tree with the trunk labeled “main” as a horizontal time axis, depth levels listed on the left (Depth 0–3), and two dashed ovals marking Branch family A (above main) and Branch family B (below main). A legend shows solid black dots as changes to foo.dll and hollow/dashed circles as changes to bar.dll; short branches of varying depths emanate from and rejoin main, with arrows labeled “Integrate” indicating merges back into the trunk. The diagram places most foo.dll changes in Branch family A (concentrated at shallower depths) while bar.dll changes are split across families A and B and deeper branches, illustrating the paper’s concepts of branch scatter and branch‑depth distribution (entropy) that the authors use to reason about integration risk and post‑release failures. The figure visually supports the branch activity, scatter, and depth metrics defined and analyzed in the study.

page6_img_1.png.title: Regression table: branching metrics' effects on Vista post-release failures
page6_img_1.png.description: This table (Table 1) presents five nested linear regression models predicting post-release failures in Windows Vista; each row is an independent variable (many log-transformed) and arrows indicate the direction of a statistically significant effect (↑ increases failures, ↓ decreases failures, - not included or not significant). Core control variables—log(Size), log(Churn), log(Dev. Changes) and log(No. Files)—all show positive associations with failures, while log(Complexity) is absent/not significant. Adding branching metrics shows Branch Activity, log(Branch Scatter), Branch Scatter Entropy and Low Branch Depth with positive effects on failures, whereas Branch Depth Entropy has a negative effect; log(High Branch Depth) is not significant. Model fit improves from R2=72% (Base Model) to 75% (Model 2 with Branch Activity), 77% (Model 3 with scatter/entropy), remains 77% in Model 4, and reaches 79% in Model 5 when branch-family (Branch Groups) variables are included, indicating that branching characteristics explain additional variance in failures.

page7_img_1.png.title: Regression models for Windows 7: predictor effects and R²
page7_img_1.png.description: Table listing five linear regression models for Windows 7 post‑release failures, showing which predictors were included and whether each had a positive (↑) or negative (↓) effect; a dash indicates the variable was not in that model. The standard control variables (log(Size), log(Churn), log(Complexity), log(Dev. Changes), log(No. Files)) are present across models and consistently show positive associations with failures. Among branch-related metrics, Branch Activity is positively associated with failures when included, Branch Scatter Entropy shows a negative association when added, and Branch Groups (per‑family change counts) has a positive effect and—when included in Model 5—substantially increases adjusted R². Model fit rises from 17% for the base model to 18–19% when activity/scatter metrics are added, then jumps to 36% in Model 5 after replacing development-change count with branch family (Branch Groups), indicating branch-family information explains much additional variance.

page7_img_3.png.title: Effect of branch scatter entropy on post-release defects (Windows 7)
page7_img_3.png.description: Line chart showing the modeled change in post-release defects (y-axis, percent of median) as Branch Scatter Entropy increases from its minimum through median to maximum (x-axis). The solid black line is the model prediction, with green dashed and red dotted lines showing the 95% confidence bounds. The model predicts a clear decline in defects as scatter entropy rises: at the minimum entropy the projected defect rate is well above the median (roughly 120–160% depending on the confidence bound), while at the maximum entropy it falls to about 80–100% of the median. This indicates that, in the paper’s Windows 7 regression, higher branch scatter entropy (changes distributed more evenly across branch families) is associated with fewer post-release failures according to the fitted model.
